cells.tense: Right now, something new is coming through the door and you're meeting it with open hands.
cells.verb: tending what has only just begun
cells.place: at the threshold where new things arrive
cells.ask: If you want it: let one thing you've tended come to its finish, and set it down on purpose — not because it failed, but because it's done. What comes back is care that doesn't run you dry, and room at the door for the next thing.
cells.core:
Right now, something new is coming through the door and you're meeting it with open hands. You're tending what has only just begun — giving it conditions, not instructions — and you're doing it without wringing yourself out. That's rare. Most people grip what's new, or ignore it; you're holding it loosely enough that it can become what it is.

If you want it: let one thing you've tended come to its finish, and set it down on purpose — not because it failed, but because it's done. What comes back is care that doesn't run you dry, and room at the door for the next thing.
cells.sheetLine: Something new is arriving and you're tending it without gripping it.

cells.tense: You're already living in the version where this turns out right, and you're bracing to make sure it does.
cells.verb: tending what has only just begun
cells.place: at the threshold where new things arrive
cells.ask: Offer: let what's arriving stay unnamed for a week. Take one step toward it with only enough light for that step, no picture of where it ends. What comes back is growth that happens without your hands around its throat — care that holds, and doesn't clutch.
cells.core:
You're already living in the version where this turns out right, and you're bracing to make sure it does. Something new has arrived and you've started tending it before you know what it is — deciding what it'll become, what it'll need, what could go wrong, all at once. The care is real. But it's arriving as pressure, and something that's just come through the door can't grow under that much hovering.

Offer: let what's arriving stay unnamed for a week. Take one step toward it with only enough light for that step, no picture of where it ends. What comes back is growth that happens without your hands around its throat — care that holds, and doesn't clutch.
cells.sheetLine: You're deciding what it'll become before it's had a chance to arrive.

cells.tense: Something came to the door a while back, and you let it wait there, and you're still standing where you were when it knocked.
cells.verb: tending what has only just begun
cells.place: at the threshold where new things arrive
cells.ask: Offer — and not the obvious one. Don't try to care harder; that's the empty tank. Instead, name one thing you actually want to see grow, out loud, to yourself, without deciding whether you'll tend it. Let the wanting lead. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust, because it's pointed at something you chose.
cells.core:
Something came to the door a while back, and you let it wait there, and you're still standing where you were when it knocked. Nothing new is being let in far enough to grow. It can look like self-sufficiency from the outside — you don't need much, you don't fuss over things — but underneath, the ground isn't taking seed. Not because nothing's arriving. Because nothing's being tended once it does.

Offer — and not the obvious one. Don't try to care harder; that's the empty tank. Instead, name one thing you actually want to see grow, out loud, to yourself, without deciding whether you'll tend it. Let the wanting lead. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust, because it's pointed at something you chose.
cells.sheetLine: New things arrive and nothing takes root — it's not independence, it's the door left shut.

cells.tense: You're the one people bring new things to, and you're already growing them, and you'd never say that's what you do.
cells.verb: tending what has only just begun
cells.place: at the threshold where new things arrive
cells.ask: Offer: pick one thing you're tending that you never agreed to pick up. Set it down — not angrily, just put it back. See if the sky falls. What comes back is care you chose, which is the only kind that doesn't drain you — holding what's growing without being held hostage by it.
cells.core:
You're the one people bring new things to, and you're already growing them, and you'd never say that's what you do. Whatever shows up at the door — their half-formed plan, their new worry, the project no one owns — ends up in your hands, getting tended. They experience you as the one who makes things grow. You experience it as being tired for no reason you can name. The tending is yours. The choosing hasn't been.

Offer: pick one thing you're tending that you never agreed to pick up. Set it down — not angrily, just put it back. See if the sky falls. What comes back is care you chose, which is the only kind that doesn't drain you — holding what's growing without being held hostage by it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already everyone's gardener. You just haven't agreed to the job.
